summary: Surveys use of IPv4 addresses in IETF Security Area standards-track and experimental documents, to find dependencies on IPv4. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A checklist of security rules that mention old-style addresses, so they can be updated.

questions: ipv4 dependencies in security area specs
subtitle: A catalog of IPv4 address dependencies in security standards.

tldr.problem: Many IETF security standards were written when IPv4 was the only IP version, creating dependencies that could hinder the transition to IPv6.
tldr.mechanism: This document systematically surveys all standards-track and experimental RFCs in the Security Area, documenting which ones contain IPv4-specific provisions and which remain address-independent.
tldr.outcome: It identified only 4 out of 124 RFCs with significant IPv4 dependencies, most of which were already being addressed by updated specifications or working groups.

today: RFC 3792 is Informational and documents the state of IPv6 readiness in 2004. Most identified issues have since been addressed through IPv6-aware updates such as RFC 3162 for RADIUS and RFC 2460 for IPv6 specification. The document remains a historical reference for understanding which security standards required attention for full IPv6 support.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This survey document is part of a broader effort to understand IPv6 readiness across IETF standards. Rather than trying to update all standards at once, the IETF divided this work by area, and this RFC focuses on the Security Area. The Security Area covers authentication, encryption, key management, and protection mechanisms that secure internet communications.

The goal is not to force immediate changes, but to identify which security protocols and standards still assume IPv4 addressing or other IPv4-specific features, so they can be updated as needed when IPv6 deployment requires it.
sections.eli5: This is a report that checks all the security rules to see which ones only work with old-style internet addresses.

sections.title: Scope and Method
sections.content:
The document surveys 124 security-related RFCs: 1 Full Standard, 3 Draft Standards, 102 Proposed Standards, and 18 Experimental RFCs. Each RFC is examined in isolation to determine whether it contains text specifically requiring IPv4 addresses, IPv4-only algorithms, or IPv4-specific header formats. The analysis is raw and unfiltered—a standard is flagged if it has any IPv4 reference, regardless of whether a fix has already been published elsewhere.

The 124 RFCs examined span topics including authentication protocols, encryption methods, key exchange mechanisms, email security, remote access services, and cryptographic algorithms.
sections.eli5: The document looks at 124 security rules one at a time, checking each one to see if it requires old-style addresses.

sections.title: Key Findings
sections.content:
The survey found only 4 RFCs with significant IPv4 dependencies out of 124 total—less than 4 percent. The findings broke down as: 0 out of 1 Full Standard (0%), 1 out of 3 Draft Standards (RADIUS, RFC 2865), 1 out of 102 Proposed Standards, and 2 out of 18 Experimental RFCs. Most security mechanisms, such as IPsec, TLS, Kerberos, and SASL, are either version-independent or already support both IPv4 and IPv6.

The main IPv4-dependent areas identified were RADIUS attribute definitions (which use 32-bit address fields) and RIP routing security (which is tied to an IPv4-only protocol). Many of the flagged standards were already being updated by their respective working groups.
sections.eli5: Only 4 out of 124 security rules have problems with old-style addresses. Most security methods don't care which version of internet addresses you use.

sections.title: Issues and Resolution
sections.content:
For RADIUS (RFC 2865), the issues were resolved through RFC 3162, which provides IPv6 extensions. The RIPv2 MD5 Authentication (RFC 2082) issue was addressed by moving to IPsec (RFC 2402), a version-independent security architecture. Mobile IPv4-related authentication extensions and DHCP authentication issues were being handled through mobile IPv6 and DHCPv6 updates, respectively.

Many standards listed had no IPv4 dependencies at all—they operate on data streams, headers, or cryptographic operations without reference to IP version. Standards that do reference addresses typically allow implementations to support both IPv4 and IPv6 with minimal changes.
sections.eli5: Most of the problems found were already being fixed by other groups. Security rules that do care about addresses can usually be updated without rewriting the whole rule.

sections.title: Status Today
sections.content:
RFC 3792 is an Informational document that remains valid. The transition to IPv6 does not require wholesale rewriting of security standards—most are already address-independent or have published IPv6-aware updates. The survey confirms that the Security Area was well-designed with version independence in mind, with only a few protocols tied to IPv4 by necessity rather than design.

For any organization deploying IPv6, this document serves as a reference to check which security standards might need supplementary specifications or extensions to fully support both address families.
sections.eli5: Most security rules work fine with both old and new address styles. A few had to be updated, but that was already happening.
